slides.title: What is a lemonade stand?
slides.text: A lemonade stand is a small business. You make lemonade, choose a price, and sell cups to people who want a drink. If someone gives you $1 for a cup, you just made a sale!

widgetConfig.scenario: You make lemonade, choose a price, and sell cups to people walking by. What is this an example of?

options.label: A small business
options.outcome: Exactly right! A lemonade stand is a small business — you make lemonade, choose a price, and sell it.

options.label: A chore
options.outcome: This is more than a chore — selling something you made for a price is a small business.

options.label: A game with no real purpose
options.outcome: It's not just a game — a lemonade stand is a genuine small business with a real purpose.

slides.title: Where ideas come from
slides.text: Business ideas can start by noticing what people need or want. If people at the park are hot and thirsty, selling cold lemonade could be a useful idea.

widgetConfig.scenario: People at the park look hot and thirsty on a sunny day. What's a business idea this could inspire?

options.label: Selling cold lemonade
options.outcome: Exactly! Noticing what people need or want, like a cold drink on a hot day, is exactly how good business ideas start.

options.label: Selling umbrellas in the desert with no customers around
options.outcome: That idea doesn't match what people actually need in that moment — noticing a real, nearby need works much better.

options.label: Ignoring it since it's not your problem
options.outcome: Noticing a need like this is exactly the kind of observation that can turn into a good business idea.

slides.title: You can make things too!
slides.text: Kids can create things that other people may want to buy. You might make bracelets, drawings, bookmarks, or cookies. Creating and selling something is one way to be an entrepreneur.

widgetConfig.scenario: You like making bracelets. Could you turn that into a tiny business?

options.label: Yes! You could sell bracelets you make to others
options.outcome: Exactly right! Kids can create things like bracelets or drawings that other people may want to buy.

options.label: No, only grown-ups can sell things they make
options.outcome: Kids can make and sell things too, like bracelets or drawings — it's a great way to start learning about business.

options.label: Only toys bought from a store count as things to sell
options.outcome: Things you make yourself, like bracelets, absolutely count — many young entrepreneurs start exactly that way.

slides.title: It takes effort
slides.text: A business does not run by itself. You may need to make the lemonade, set up the table, create a sign, and clean up afterward. That work is part of being an entrepreneur.

widgetConfig.prompt: Which of these is NOT part of running a lemonade stand?

items.label: Waiting for money to appear by itself

widgetConfig.explanation: Money doesn't appear by itself — a business takes real effort, like making the lemonade, setting up, and making a sign.

slides.title: Making something to sell
slides.text: Before you can sell something, you need to make or prepare it. For lemonade, you might mix lemons, water, and sugar, then pour it into cups for customers.

widgetConfig.scenario: Before you can sell lemonade, what do you need to do first?

options.label: Make or prepare the lemonade
options.outcome: Exactly right! Before you can sell something, you need to make or prepare it first.

options.label: Just put out an empty table
options.outcome: An empty table has nothing to sell — you need to actually make the lemonade first.

options.label: Wait for lemonade to appear on its own
options.outcome: Lemonade doesn't appear on its own — you need to make or prepare it.

slides.title: What is trading?
slides.text: Trading means exchanging one thing for another. At a lemonade stand, a customer gives you money and you give them lemonade. Both people receive something they value.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have extra stickers and your friend has an extra toy car you want. What could you do?

options.label: Trade your stickers for their toy car, if you both agree
options.outcome: Exactly! Trading is when two people swap things they both agree to exchange.

options.label: Just take the toy car
options.outcome: Taking isn't trading — trading means both people agree to the swap.

options.label: Ignore it since you can't trade
options.outcome: You can trade! Just ask if they'd like to swap something for your stickers.

slides.title: Who is a customer?
slides.text: A customer is a person who buys something from a business. If your neighbor pays for a cup of lemonade, your neighbor is your customer.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your neighbor pays you for a cup of lemonade. What do we call your neighbor?

options.label: A customer
options.outcome: Exactly right! A customer is a person who buys something from a business, like your neighbor buying lemonade.

options.label: An employee
options.outcome: An employee works for the business — someone who buys from it is called a customer.

options.label: A competitor
options.outcome: A competitor runs a similar business — someone who buys from you is called a customer.

slides.title: A happy customer comes back
slides.text: When customers like what they bought and are treated kindly, they may come back again. A neighbor who loved your lemonade today might buy another cup tomorrow.

widgetConfig.scenario: A customer buys lemonade from your stand and says it was delicious. What's likely to happen next?

options.label: They might come back again, and maybe bring friends
options.outcome: Yes! Happy customers often return and tell others — that's great for your stand.

options.label: They'll never think about your stand again
options.outcome: Happy customers often remember and come back — making customers happy is really important for a business.

options.label: It doesn't matter if they're happy or not
options.outcome: It matters a lot! Happy customers are more likely to return and tell their friends.

quiz.question: What is a lemonade stand?
choices: A tiny business selling lemonade
A place to take a nap
quiz.explanation: A lemonade stand is a small business. You make lemonade and sell cups to customers. If someone pays $1 for a cup, that is a sale.

quiz.question: What is a customer?
choices: Someone who buys what you're selling
A type of lemon
quiz.explanation: A customer is someone who buys something from you. If your neighbor pays for lemonade, your neighbor is your customer.

quiz.question: You give lemonade, and get a coin. What just happened?
choices: You traded — you both gave and got something
Nothing happened at all
quiz.explanation: You made an exchange: the customer gave you money, and you gave the customer lemonade. That is a simple trade.

quiz.question: Where do business ideas often come from?
choices: Noticing something people want or need
They only come from grown-ups, never kids
quiz.explanation: Business ideas often start by noticing what people need or want. Thirsty people on a hot day might want a cold drink.

quiz.question: Does running a lemonade stand take effort?
choices: Yes, it takes real work
No, it happens by itself
quiz.explanation: Yes. You may need to make lemonade, carry supplies, create a sign, serve customers, and clean up afterward.

quiz.question: What must you do before selling lemonade?
choices: Make it first, with lemons, sugar, and water
You can sell it before it exists
quiz.explanation: You need something ready to sell. For lemonade, that means making the drink and getting cups ready before customers arrive.

quiz.question: What happens when a customer loves your lemonade?
choices: They often come back to buy more
They never think about it again
quiz.explanation: A happy customer may come back or tell someone else about your stand. Treating customers well can help a small business grow.

quiz.question: You notice kids at the park are very thirsty on a hot day. What's a good idea?
choices: Start a lemonade stand for them
Sell them mittens
quiz.explanation: A lemonade stand could solve a simple problem: thirsty people want a cold drink. Good business ideas often start by noticing a need.

quiz.question: What is one thing you could make to sell, besides lemonade?
choices: Bracelets, drawings, or cookies
A cloud
quiz.explanation: You can create many things people may want, such as bracelets, drawings, bookmarks, or cookies. Making and selling something is one way to start a small business.

quiz.question: Can kids have good business ideas, or only grown-ups?
choices: Kids can have great ideas too
Only grown-ups can have ideas
quiz.explanation: Kids can notice problems, create things, and think of useful ideas too. A business idea can start with anyone who spots a need and thinks of a solution.

slides.title: Picking a fair price
slides.text: A price is how much money someone pays for what you sell. A fair price should make sense for both you and the customer. For example, you might charge $1 for one cold cup of lemonade.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're deciding how much to charge for one cup of lemonade. What makes a price fair?

options.label: It makes sense for both you and the customer
options.outcome: Exactly right! A fair price should make sense for both you and the customer, not just one side.

options.label: As expensive as possible, no matter what
options.outcome: Charging as much as possible, no matter what, isn't fair to the customer — a good price works for both sides.

options.label: Free, so you never make any money
options.outcome: Giving it away for free means your business never earns anything — a fair price works for both you and the customer.

slides.title: Telling people about your stand
slides.text: People cannot buy from your stand if they do not know it is there. A bright sign saying “Lemonade $1” can help neighbors notice what you are selling.

widgetConfig.scenario: You set up a lemonade stand, but nobody knows it's there. What should you do?

options.label: Make a sign or tell people about it
options.outcome: Exactly right! People cannot buy from your stand if they do not know it is there — telling people helps.

options.label: Just wait quietly and hope people notice
options.outcome: Waiting quietly means people may never notice — making a sign or telling people helps far more.

options.label: Customers always find stands automatically with no effort
options.outcome: Customers don't just find stands automatically — telling people about it helps a lot.

slides.title: Counting your coins
slides.text: At the end of the day, count the money you received. If you sold five cups for $1 each, you collected $5. Keeping track helps you understand how your business did.

widgetConfig.scenario: You sold five cups of lemonade for $1 each. How much money did you collect?

options.outcome: Exactly right! Five cups at $1 each adds up to $5.
That's the price of just one cup — five cups at $1 each adds up to $5 total.
That would be if cups cost $2 each — at $1 each, five cups adds up to $5.

slides.title: Saving up for supplies
slides.text: A business may need supplies to keep going. Saving some of the money you earn can help you buy more lemons, cups, or ice for the next day.

widgetConfig.scenario: You earn money from your lemonade stand. Why might you save some of it instead of spending it all?

options.label: To buy more lemons, cups, or ice for next time
options.outcome: Exactly right! Saving some of what you earn helps you buy more supplies to keep your business going.

options.label: Saving never helps a business
options.outcome: Saving actually helps a lot — it lets you buy supplies to keep your business running.

options.label: You should always spend every cent immediately
options.outcome: Spending everything immediately leaves nothing for next time's supplies — saving some helps your business continue.

slides.title: Saving some, spending some
slides.text: You do not have to spend all the money you earn. You can save some for a goal, keep some for your business, and spend some later.

slides.title: Being honest
slides.text: Honesty helps people trust you. If your lemonade is warm or you ran out of a flavor, tell the truth instead of pretending. Customers appreciate honest sellers.

widgetConfig.scenario: A customer gives you too much change by accident at your lemonade stand. What's the right thing to do?

options.label: Point it out and give back the extra change
options.outcome: That's exactly right! Being honest, even when it costs you a little, builds trust and a good reputation for your business.

options.label: Keep the extra money quietly
options.outcome: Keeping money that isn't yours isn't honest — pointing it out builds trust with customers.

options.label: Only give it back if they notice
options.outcome: Being honest means doing the right thing even if no one would notice otherwise.

slides.title: Teamwork with a friend
slides.text: Two people can share the work. One friend might pour lemonade while the other greets customers and collects money. Teamwork can make a busy stand easier to run.

widgetConfig.scenario: Running a busy lemonade stand alone is hard. How can a friend help?

options.label: Share the work, like pouring while the other greets customers
options.outcome: Exactly right! Two people can share the work, which can make a busy stand much easier to run.

options.label: Having a friend around never helps
options.outcome: A friend sharing the work can actually make a busy stand much easier to manage.

options.label: Only one person should ever be allowed to help
options.outcome: Sharing the work between two people is exactly what makes a busy stand easier to run.

slides.title: A slow day happens sometimes
slides.text: Some days you may sell a lot, and other days you may sell only a little. One slow day does not mean your idea is bad. You can think about what to change and try again.

widgetConfig.scenario: You barely sold any lemonade today. Does this mean your business idea is bad?

options.label: No — one slow day doesn't mean the idea is bad
options.outcome: Exactly right! One slow day does not mean your idea is bad — you can think about what to change and try again.

options.label: Yes, you should give up immediately
options.outcome: A single slow day isn't a reason to quit — thinking about what to change and trying again is a better response.

options.label: Slow days never happen to good businesses
options.outcome: Slow days happen to good businesses too — one slow day doesn't mean the idea itself is bad.

slides.title: Cleaning up your stand
slides.text: Good business owners take care of their space. After selling, throw away trash, put supplies away, and leave the area clean for everyone.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're done selling for the day. What should a good business owner do?

options.label: Clean up the trash and put supplies away
options.outcome: Exactly right! Good business owners take care of their space by cleaning up and putting supplies away.

options.label: Leave the mess for someone else
options.outcome: Leaving a mess isn't taking care of your space — cleaning up yourself is what a good business owner does.

options.label: Cleaning up doesn't matter at all
options.outcome: Cleaning up actually matters — it shows you take care of your space and respect the people around you.

quiz.question: What makes a price fair?
choices: Not too high and not too low
As high as you can possibly charge
quiz.explanation: A fair price makes sense for both the seller and the customer. For example, $1 for a cold cup may feel reasonable if it covers the cost and the customer is happy to pay it.

quiz.question: Why make a big sign for your stand?
choices: So people notice your stand and stop by
To keep the sun off your lemonade
quiz.explanation: A clear sign helps people notice what you are selling and how much it costs. If people do not see your stand, they may walk right past it.

quiz.question: Two friends run a lemonade stand. What's a good way to work together?
choices: Share the jobs, like pouring cups and collecting coins
One friend does nothing at all
quiz.explanation: Sharing jobs makes the work easier. One person could pour lemonade while the other greets customers and collects money.

quiz.question: Why count your coins at the end of the day?
choices: To know how much you earned
To build a tall tower
quiz.explanation: Counting your money tells you how much you collected. If you sold five cups for $1 each, you should have collected $5.

quiz.question: What's a good idea to do with your earnings?
choices: Save some and spend some
Hide them and forget about them
quiz.explanation: You can divide your money for different goals: save some, use some for more supplies, and spend some later.

quiz.question: Your lemonade is a little warm today. What should you tell a customer?
choices: The truth, that it's a bit warm
Nothing, just sell it anyway
quiz.explanation: Tell the truth. Honest sellers build trust, and customers are more likely to return when they know they can believe you.

quiz.question: No one stops by your stand today. What should you do?
choices: Try again another day
Give up on your stand forever
quiz.explanation: One slow day does not mean you should quit. You can try again and think about whether a different time, sign, or location might help.

quiz.question: Why clean up your stand after selling?
choices: It makes the spot tidy for your neighbors
It makes the lemonade taste better
quiz.explanation: Cleaning up shows responsibility. It keeps the area pleasant for neighbors and gets your supplies ready for next time.

quiz.question: If you save $1 today and $1 tomorrow, how much have you saved?
quiz.explanation: You saved $2 because $1 + $1 = $2. Small amounts can grow when you keep saving.

quiz.question: What helps a customer trust you?
choices: Being honest with them
Never talking to them
quiz.explanation: Being honest and kind helps customers trust you. Trust makes people more comfortable buying from you again.

slides.title: Spotting a problem to solve
slides.text: Good business ideas often start when you notice a problem, like no cold drinks at the park. That kind of gap, noticed on a hot day, could become your very own business idea.

widgetConfig.scenario: You notice nobody at the park has a cold drink on a hot day. What's a smart first step for a business idea?

options.label: Notice that problem — it could be the start of a good business idea
options.outcome: Exactly! Good business ideas often start when you notice a problem, like people wanting a cold drink on a hot day.

options.label: Ignore it since problems have nothing to do with business ideas
options.outcome: Problems are actually where many good business ideas start — noticing one is a smart first step.

options.label: Only huge, famous problems can ever lead to a business idea
options.outcome: Small, everyday problems, like no cold drinks at the park, can lead to great business ideas too.

slides.title: Cost vs. price
slides.text: Cost is what you spend to make or get a product. Price is what a customer pays you for it. If a cup of lemonade costs 20¢ to make and you sell it for $1, the difference before any other expenses is 80¢.

widgetConfig.scenario: It costs you $0.30 to make a cup of lemonade (cups, lemons, sugar). If you sell each cup for $0.30, do you make a profit?

options.label: No — you need to charge more than your cost to make a profit
options.outcome: Exactly right — if your price equals your cost, you break even with no profit. You need to charge more than it costs to make money.

options.label: Yes, selling at cost is a smart business move
options.outcome: Selling at exactly your cost means you make $0 profit — you need to price above your cost to actually earn money.

options.label: It doesn't matter what price you charge
options.outcome: Price matters a lot! Charging less than or equal to your cost means you won't make any profit.

slides.title: A simple plan
slides.text: Before starting, it helps to plan what you'll sell, what it costs, and what you'll charge. Writing down a plan, like charging a dollar for 20-cent lemonade, avoids confusion later.

widgetConfig.prompt: Tap the planning steps in the right order

slides.title: Giving your business a name
slides.text: A fun, memorable name helps people remember your stand and tell their friends about it. Calling your stand "Sam's Sunny Lemonade" sticks in people's minds much better than having no name at all.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're starting a lemonade stand. Why might giving it a memorable name help?

options.label: It helps people remember your stand and tell friends
options.outcome: Exactly right! A fun, memorable name helps people remember your stand and tell their friends about it.

options.label: Names never matter for a business
options.outcome: A good name actually helps a lot — it makes your stand memorable and easier for people to recommend.

options.label: A confusing name attracts more customers
options.outcome: A confusing name tends to be forgotten, not remembered — a clear, fun name works much better.

slides.title: Making your product special
slides.text: Adding something unique, like a flavor nobody else has, can make customers choose your stand. A splash of strawberry or mint, something other stands don't offer, could set you apart.

widgetConfig.scenario: Lots of other stands sell plain lemonade. What could help yours stand out?

options.label: Adding a unique flavor nobody else offers
options.outcome: Exactly! Adding something unique, like a flavor nobody else has, can make customers choose your stand.

options.label: Making it exactly the same as everyone else
options.outcome: Being exactly the same as everyone else doesn't give customers a reason to pick your stand specifically.

options.label: Uniqueness never matters to customers
options.outcome: Uniqueness actually matters a lot — it's often exactly what makes customers choose one stand over another.

slides.title: Checking what others charge
slides.text: Before choosing a price, it helps to see what similar sellers charge and what customers are willing to pay. You do not always have to be cheaper — better quality, flavor, or service can also make your product worth choosing.

widgetConfig.scenario: Before setting your lemonade price, you notice a nearby stand charges $1 per cup. What should you do?

options.label: Consider that price when setting your own, so you're competitive
options.outcome: Smart move! Checking what others charge helps you set a fair, competitive price for your own product.

options.label: Ignore other prices completely
options.outcome: Knowing what others charge helps you set a smart, competitive price — ignoring it could mean pricing too high or too low.

options.label: Charge way more just to seem fancy
options.outcome: Pricing way above competitors without a good reason can mean fewer customers — it's smart to consider the market price.

slides.title: Picking a good spot
slides.text: Where you set up your stand matters just as much as what you're selling. A spot near a park entrance or a busy sidewalk, where lots of people walk by, will get far more customers than a hidden corner of your yard.

widgetConfig.scenario: Where should you set up your lemonade stand for the most customers?

options.label: Somewhere busy, like near a park entrance
options.outcome: Exactly right! A spot where lots of people walk by will get far more customers than a hidden corner.

options.label: A hidden corner of your yard
options.outcome: A hidden spot means fewer people will notice your stand — a busy location gets far more customers.

options.label: Location never affects how many customers you get
options.outcome: Location actually matters a lot — a busy spot gets far more customers than a hidden one.

slides.title: Planning your day
slides.text: Deciding when to open and how much to make ahead of time helps your day run smoothly. Planning to open from 2 to 4pm with 20 cups ready means you won't scramble later.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want your stand to run smoothly. What helps?

options.label: Deciding when to open and how much to make ahead of time
options.outcome: Exactly! Planning to open at a set time with enough cups ready helps your day run smoothly.

options.label: Figuring it out randomly as you go
options.outcome: Figuring it out randomly tends to cause scrambling later — planning ahead helps things run smoothly.

options.label: Planning ahead never helps a business
options.outcome: Planning ahead actually helps a lot — it prevents scrambling and keeps your day running smoothly.

quiz.question: What does "spot a problem" mean for a business idea?
choices: Noticing something people need that isn't available
Finding a hole in your sock
quiz.explanation: A business idea often starts when you notice something people need but don't have, like cold drinks missing from a hot, crowded park. Spotting that gap is the first step.

quiz.question: A cup of lemonade costs 20 cents to make and sells for $1. What is your profit on that cup?
choices: 80 cents
quiz.explanation: Profit is what's left after you subtract your cost from your price. Lemonade that costs 20 cents to make and sells for $1 leaves you 80 cents of profit.

quiz.question: Why is a simple plan helpful before starting a business?
choices: It helps you figure out what to sell and for how much
Plans are only for grown-ups
quiz.explanation: A simple plan, like deciding lemonade costs 20 cents and sells for $1, helps you think things through before you start selling. It stops confusion later.

quiz.question: How can adding a unique flavor to your lemonade help your business?
choices: It can make customers pick you over other sellers
It never makes any difference
quiz.explanation: Adding something special, like a strawberry or mint flavor nobody else has, gives customers a reason to pick your stand over another one. It helps you stand out.

quiz.question: Why is it helpful to plan your day before opening a stand?
choices: It helps the whole day run more smoothly
Planning ahead never actually helps
quiz.explanation: Deciding your hours and how much to make ahead, like opening 2 to 4pm with 20 cups ready, keeps your day from feeling rushed.

quiz.question: Why check what other nearby stands charge before setting your own price?
choices: It helps you set a price customers will actually choose
It doesn't matter at all what others charge
quiz.explanation: Checking what nearby sellers charge helps you pick a price customers will actually pay. If everyone else charges $1, charging close to that feels fair to buyers.

quiz.question: Why give your stand a fun, memorable name?
choices: It helps people remember and recognize your stand
Names don't matter for a lemonade stand
quiz.explanation: A fun name, like "Sam's Sunny Lemonade," helps people remember your stand and tell their friends about it. A forgettable stand is easy to overlook.

quiz.question: Why does where you set up your stand matter?
choices: A busy spot means more people can see and buy
Location never makes any difference
quiz.explanation: Where you set up matters as much as what you sell, because a busy spot near a park entrance gets seen by way more people than a hidden corner of your yard.

quiz.question: Lemonade costs 30 cents to make and sells for 75 cents. What's the profit?
choices: 45 cents
105 cents
quiz.explanation: Profit is the price you charge minus what it cost to make. Selling lemonade for 75 cents that cost 30 cents to make leaves you 45 cents of profit.

quiz.question: What should a simple business plan include?
choices: What you'll sell, what it costs, and what you'll charge
Just your name and nothing else
quiz.explanation: A simple business plan covers three basics: what you're selling, what it costs you, and what price you'll charge. Skipping any one of these can cause confusion later.

slides.title: Good customer service
slides.text: Being friendly, honest, and helpful makes people want to buy from you again. When a customer asks for less sugar and you happily make it their way, they often return.

widgetConfig.scenario: A customer asks for less sugar in their lemonade. What should you do?

options.label: Happily make it their way
options.outcome: Exactly right! When you happily make a drink the way a customer wants it, they often return.

options.label: Refuse and make it the same for everyone
options.outcome: Refusing a reasonable request can make a customer less likely to return — happily adjusting works much better.

options.label: Customer requests never matter
options.outcome: Customer requests actually matter a lot — happily meeting them is part of good customer service.

slides.title: Telling people about it
slides.text: Even a great product needs people to know it exists, which is called marketing. A bright poster that says "Cold Lemonade, $1!" lets passing neighbors know your stand is open.

widgetConfig.scenario: You started a dog-walking business but nobody knows about it yet. What should you do?

options.label: Tell neighbors and friends, maybe make a simple flyer
options.outcome: Great idea! Telling people about your business, even informally, helps customers find you.

options.label: Wait for customers to magically find you
options.outcome: Customers usually need to hear about your business first — telling people helps a lot.

options.label: Keep it a secret
options.outcome: A secret business won't get customers — telling people is how they find out you exist!

slides.title: Keeping track
slides.text: Writing down the money that comes in and the money you spend helps you understand whether your business is working. If you earned $12 and spent $4 on supplies, you have $8 left before any other expenses.

widgetConfig.scenario: You earned $12 and spent $4 on supplies. How much do you have left before other expenses?

options.outcome: Exactly right! $12 earned minus $4 spent leaves you with $8.
That's before subtracting your $4 in supply costs — you'd have $8 left after spending.
That would mean adding instead of subtracting — $12 minus $4 spent leaves $8.

slides.title: Getting help from a grown-up
slides.text: Many young entrepreneurs ask a parent or grown-up for help with things like buying supplies or handling money safely. Asking your mom to drive you to buy more lemons, or having her hold onto your earnings, is a smart, normal part of running a kid business.

widgetConfig.scenario: You need to buy more lemons and want to handle money safely. What's a smart move?

options.label: Ask a parent or grown-up for help
options.outcome: Exactly right! Many young entrepreneurs ask a parent or grown-up for help with supplies or handling money safely.

options.label: Never ask a grown-up for anything
options.outcome: Asking for help with things like buying supplies or handling money is a smart, normal part of running a kid business.

options.label: Asking for help means you're not a real entrepreneur
options.outcome: Asking for help is actually a smart, normal part of running a kid business, not a sign of failure.

slides.title: Trying again if it doesn't work
slides.text: When a business idea doesn't work at first, entrepreneurs usually adjust it instead of quitting. If nobody stopped by on a cloudy day, you might try a sunnier spot next time.

widgetConfig.scenario: Nobody stopped by your stand on a cloudy day. What should you do?

options.label: Adjust and try again, like picking a sunnier spot next time
options.outcome: Exactly right! When a business idea doesn't work at first, entrepreneurs usually adjust it instead of quitting.

options.label: Quit the business forever
options.outcome: Quitting after one slow day skips a chance to adjust and improve — trying again usually works better.

options.label: Keep doing the exact same thing and expect different results
options.outcome: Repeating the exact same approach tends to get the same result — adjusting something, like your spot, helps more.

slides.title: Handling an unhappy customer
slides.text: Sometimes a customer isn't happy, maybe your lemonade seemed too sour for their taste. Listening calmly and offering a new cup, or their money back, keeps their trust.

widgetConfig.scenario: A customer says the cookie they bought from your stand wasn't very good. What's the best response?

options.label: Apologize and offer to make it right
options.outcome: Great instinct! Making it right keeps customers happy and coming back — that's good for any business.

options.label: That's not my problem.
options.outcome: Dismissing a complaint can lose you a customer for good — and they might tell their friends too.

options.label: Argue that the cookie was fine
options.outcome: Arguing with an unhappy customer rarely helps — listening and offering a fix builds trust instead.

slides.title: Splitting jobs with a partner
slides.text: Running a business with a friend works best when you split up the jobs. One person could make the lemonade while the other greets customers and handles the money.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're running a stand with a friend. What's a smart way to split the work?

options.label: One makes lemonade while the other greets customers and handles money
options.outcome: Exactly right! Splitting up the jobs, like one making lemonade and the other greeting customers, works best.

options.label: Both people should do nothing and hope it works out
options.outcome: Doing nothing doesn't run a business — splitting the actual jobs between you works much better.

options.label: Splitting jobs never helps a team
options.outcome: Splitting jobs actually helps a lot — it makes running the stand together much more manageable.

slides.title: Saving up for a goal
slides.text: Saving some of your profit each week can help you buy something bigger later on. If you save $2 every week, you'll have $20 saved after ten weeks.

widgetConfig.scenario: You earn some profit from your lemonade stand each week. How can this help you buy something bigger later?

options.label: Save some of the profit each week toward the goal
options.outcome: Exactly! Saving a portion of your profit regularly adds up over time toward a bigger goal.

options.label: Spend all the profit right away each week
options.outcome: Spending everything right away means you'll never build up enough for a bigger goal — saving some each week helps.

options.label: Wait until you have a huge amount before saving any
options.outcome: Saving a little bit regularly works better than waiting — small amounts add up toward your goal over time.

slides.title: Celebrating your progress
slides.text: Entrepreneurs can celebrate progress without spending all their earnings. Reaching a goal — like your first 10 customers — is a good reason to feel proud, share the news, or choose a small reward.

widgetConfig.scenario: You just reached your first 10 customers! What's a reasonable way to celebrate?

options.label: Feel proud, share the news, or pick a small reward
options.outcome: Exactly right! Reaching a goal like your first 10 customers is a good reason to feel proud and celebrate a little.

options.label: Spend every single cent you have earned immediately
options.outcome: Spending everything right away isn't necessary — a small reward is plenty, while saving the rest helps your business.

options.label: Progress is never worth celebrating
options.outcome: Progress is absolutely worth celebrating — it's a good way to stay motivated as an entrepreneur.

quiz.question: Why does good customer service matter?
choices: It makes customers want to come back and tell friends
It has no real effect on a business
quiz.explanation: Being friendly and helpful, like happily making lemonade with less sugar when someone asks, makes customers want to return. Good service builds trust.

quiz.question: What is marketing, in simple terms?
choices: Telling people about what you're selling
Counting your money at the end of the day
quiz.explanation: Marketing just means telling people your product exists, like hanging a bright poster that says "Cold Lemonade, $1!" so neighbors know to stop by.

quiz.question: If a business idea doesn't work at first, what do entrepreneurs usually do?
choices: Tweak the idea and try again
Never attempt anything again
quiz.explanation: When an idea flops, entrepreneurs usually tweak something and try again instead of quitting, like trying a sunnier spot after a slow, cloudy day.

quiz.question: A customer says your lemonade is too sour. What should you do?
choices: Listen calmly and offer a new cup or their money back
Ignore them and walk away
quiz.explanation: Listening calmly to an unhappy customer, like offering a new cup if your lemonade tastes too sour, keeps their trust in your business. Ignoring them usually loses a customer for good.

quiz.question: You and a friend run a stand together. What's a smart way to split the work?
choices: One makes lemonade while the other handles customers and money
Both do the exact same job at the exact same time
quiz.explanation: Splitting different jobs, like one friend making lemonade while the other handles money, makes a team work faster than both doing the same task.

quiz.question: You spent $4 on supplies and earned $12. What was your profit?
quiz.explanation: Profit is what you earn minus what you spent. Earning $12 after spending $4 on supplies leaves you an $8 profit.

quiz.question: Why is it smart to ask a grown-up for help with your business?
choices: They can help with things like buying supplies or handling money safely
Grown-ups should never be involved in a kid's business
quiz.explanation: Asking a trusted adult to help buy supplies or hold onto your earnings is smart, not embarrassing. Most young entrepreneurs get this kind of help.

quiz.question: After a great week of sales, what's a good thing to do?
choices: Celebrate your progress and feel proud
Ignore it completely and feel nothing
quiz.explanation: Pausing to celebrate, like treating yourself after a great sales week, helps you notice and feel proud of the work you did. It's not just about rushing to the next task.

quiz.question: Why keep track of what you spend and earn?
choices: It helps you see if your business is really working
Numbers don't matter for a lemonade stand
quiz.explanation: Writing down what you spend and earn shows clearly whether your business is actually making money. Without tracking it, you're just guessing.

quiz.question: You and a friend keep arguing about whose turn it is to pour cups. What might help?
choices: Agreeing ahead of time who does which job
Never talking about it and hoping it fixes itself
quiz.explanation: Agreeing ahead of time who does which job, like who pours cups, helps friends avoid arguing about it later. A clear plan prevents most disagreements.

slides.title: Knowing your customer
slides.text: Successful businesses learn who is most likely to buy from them — what those customers like, need, and can afford. For example, if classmates love fantasy books, you might design original dragon or magic-themed bookmarks rather than copying copyrighted characters.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to sell friendship bracelets. Who should you think about first?

options.label: Who would actually want to buy them, like kids your age
options.outcome: Exactly! Knowing who your customers are helps you design and price your product for them.

options.label: Just make whatever you personally like
options.outcome: Your own taste matters, but thinking about who'll actually buy it helps you design something people want.

options.label: It doesn't matter who buys them
options.outcome: It matters a lot — understanding your customers helps you make smarter choices about your product.

slides.title: Taking a smart risk
slides.text: Starting a business always involves some risk — it might not work. Smart entrepreneurs take risks they can afford, not risks that could ruin them. For example, spending $10 of your own savings to try selling friendship bracelets at a school fair is a smart, affordable risk — spending your entire year's savings on the same idea would not be.

widgetConfig.scenario: Starting any business involves some risk that it might not work out. What makes a risk 'smart' rather than careless?

options.label: Thinking it through and limiting how much you could lose
options.outcome: Exactly right! A smart risk means thinking it through and limiting how much you could lose if it doesn't work out.

options.label: Risk never matters in business
options.outcome: Risk actually matters a lot in business — the key is taking a smart, well-thought-out risk, not ignoring risk entirely.

options.label: A smart risk means risking everything you have
options.outcome: Risking everything is the opposite of smart — a smart risk limits how much you could lose.

slides.title: Finding a business idea
slides.text: Most solid business ideas start the same way — by noticing a problem or an annoying gap in what's available. For example, noticing that kids at your school have nowhere nearby to buy a cold snack after practice could turn into a snack-selling business, simply because you spotted a real, everyday need.

widgetConfig.prompt: Which of these is NOT a good way to find a business idea?

items.label: Asking friends what they wish existed
Copying something exactly, with zero changes or understanding
Thinking about what you're good at

widgetConfig.explanation: Copying something exactly without understanding why it worked rarely succeeds the same way — the other three are solid starting points for finding a real idea.

slides.title: Testing your idea small before going big
slides.text: Before investing a lot of time or money, smart entrepreneurs try a small version of their idea first to see if people actually want it. For example, making and selling just 10 candles to friends and family before ordering hundreds of dollars of supplies lets you learn what works with very little risk.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have an idea for a dog-walking business and you're excited to buy business cards, a website, and equipment right away. What's the smarter first step?

options.label: Try it small first — walk a couple of neighbors' dogs to see if people want it
options.outcome: Smart move — testing small lets you learn what works before investing a lot of time and money into something unproven.

options.label: Go all in immediately with all the big purchases
options.outcome: Going all in before testing the idea risks a lot of money on something that might not actually work as planned.

options.label: Give up before trying since it might not work
options.outcome: You don't need to give up — testing small is exactly how you find out if an idea works, without the big risk.

slides.title: Estimating startup costs
slides.text: Startup costs are the money you need to spend before your business earns anything at all, like ingredients, containers, or a sign. For example, a cookie business might need $15 for flour, sugar, and butter, plus $5 for bags and labels, meaning you'd need $20 just to get started.

widgetConfig.scenario: A cookie business needs $15 for ingredients and $5 for bags and labels. What's the total startup cost?

options.outcome: Exactly right! $15 for ingredients plus $5 for bags and labels adds up to $20 in startup costs.
That's just the ingredient cost — adding the $5 for bags and labels brings the total to $20.
That's just the bags and labels cost — adding the $15 for ingredients brings the total to $20.

slides.title: Needs vs. wants
slides.text: A need solves an important problem; a want makes life more enjoyable or convenient. Both can support good businesses. The key is understanding how strongly customers care about the problem and whether they will pay for your solution.

widgetConfig.prompt: Sort each item into Need or Want

slides.title: Writing a simple pitch
slides.text: A pitch is a short, clear explanation of your business idea that you could tell someone in under a minute. For example, "I make custom phone cases for $12 each, designed exactly how a customer wants them" tells a potential customer or helper exactly what you do and why it matters.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone asks what your business does. What makes a good pitch?

options.label: A short, clear explanation in under a minute
options.outcome: Exactly right! A pitch is a short, clear explanation of your business idea that you could tell someone in under a minute.

options.label: A long, rambling explanation with no clear point
options.outcome: A long, unclear explanation can lose someone's interest — a short, clear pitch works much better.

options.label: Refusing to explain your business at all
options.outcome: Not explaining your business at all misses the chance to interest a customer or helper — a quick pitch works better.

slides.title: Setting a goal for your first month
slides.text: Having a clear, specific goal — like earning $50 in your first month — gives you something concrete to work toward and a way to measure whether your business is on track. For example, if you're only halfway to your goal by week three, that's a signal to try something new, like a better sign or a new selling spot.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're only halfway to your $50 goal by week three of the month. What should this tell you?

options.label: It's a signal to try something new, like a better sign or spot
options.outcome: Exactly right! Falling behind your goal partway through is a signal to try something new, not just hope it fixes itself.

options.label: Nothing — goals don't matter once set
options.outcome: Goals actually matter a lot — checking your progress against them tells you when to adjust your approach.

options.label: You should give up on the goal completely
options.outcome: Falling behind doesn't mean giving up — it's a signal to try something new, like a better sign or selling spot.

quiz.question: Why does it help to understand your customer?
choices: So you can offer what they actually want and can afford
It doesn't matter who buys your product
quiz.explanation: Understanding your customer helps you design something they actually want, price it appropriately, and explain why it is useful. For example, if classmates enjoy fantasy stories, original magic-themed bookmarks may appeal more than generic designs.

quiz.question: Which is a "smart risk" for a young entrepreneur?
choices: Spending $10 of savings to try selling bracelets at a fair
Spending your entire year of savings on one untested idea
quiz.explanation: A smart risk is one you can afford to lose, not one that could wipe you out. Spending $10 of savings to try selling bracelets at a fair is affordable; spending your entire year's savings on the same untested idea is not.

quiz.question: What's a smart way to find a business idea?
choices: Notice a problem or need people have
Randomly pick anything with no thought
quiz.explanation: Many strong business ideas start by noticing a real, everyday problem, like kids at school having no nearby way to buy a cold snack after practice. Spotting that gap can turn into an actual business.

quiz.question: Before launching a big version of your idea, why test it small first?
choices: It lets you learn and fix problems while risking less money
Testing small is a waste of time and should be skipped
quiz.explanation: Testing a small version of your idea, like selling just 10 candles to friends and family, lets you learn what works before spending hundreds of dollars on supplies. It's a low-risk way to check demand.

quiz.question: What are "startup costs"?
choices: The money needed to get a business going before it earns anything
Money a business earns after several successful years
quiz.explanation: Startup costs are the expenses you pay before your business earns anything, like ingredients or a sign. A cookie business might need $15 for flour, sugar, and butter plus $5 for bags, meaning $20 just to begin.

quiz.question: Which is an example of solving a genuine need rather than a passing want?
choices: Tutoring students who are struggling in math
Selling a trendy toy just because it's popular this month
quiz.explanation: Tutoring can solve an ongoing problem for students who need help learning math. A trendy toy may still be a valid business, but demand could disappear faster if the trend fades.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to write a simple pitch for your business idea?
choices: It helps you clearly explain your idea to customers or helpers
Pitches are only useful for huge, established companies
quiz.explanation: A pitch is a short, clear explanation of your business you could say in under a minute, like "I make custom phone cases for $12 each, designed how the customer wants." It quickly tells someone what you do and why it matters.

quiz.question: Why set a specific goal, like earning $50, for your first month?
choices: It gives you something concrete to work toward and measure
Goals only matter for adult businesses, not kid ones
quiz.explanation: Setting a specific goal, like earning $50 in your first month, gives you something to measure your progress against. If you're only halfway there by week three, that's a signal to try something new, like a better sign or spot.

quiz.question: Your customers are mostly classmates who love a certain book series. What might you do?
choices: Design products, like bookmarks, featuring those characters
Ignore their interests and sell something unrelated
quiz.explanation: Understanding your customers well, like knowing classmates love a certain book series, helps you design products they're genuinely excited about, such as bookmarks featuring those characters instead of something random.

quiz.question: You're starting a dog-walking business. Which of these is a startup cost?
choices: A leash or bags you need to buy before your first walk
Money you'll earn after three months of walking dogs
quiz.explanation: Startup costs are the expenses you pay before the business earns a cent, like a leash or bags for a dog-walking business. Money you earn later, after months of walking dogs, is revenue, not a startup cost.

slides.title: Pricing fairly
slides.text: A fair price should cover your costs, reward your time and effort, and still make sense to customers. If a bracelet uses $3 of materials, you might test an $8 price and see whether buyers think the quality and design are worth it.

widgetConfig.scenario: A bracelet uses $3 of materials. You're testing an $8 price. What should a fair price do?

options.label: Cover costs, reward your effort, and still make sense to customers
options.outcome: Exactly right! A fair price should cover your costs, reward your time and effort, and still make sense to customers.

options.label: Be as high as possible no matter what
options.outcome: Pricing as high as possible regardless of value can push customers away — a fair price balances costs, effort, and customer value.

options.label: Ignore your costs completely
options.outcome: Ignoring your costs could mean losing money on every sale — a fair price needs to at least cover what you spent.

slides.title: Standing out from competitors
slides.text: When several businesses sell similar things, customers need a reason to choose one. You could stand out through better quality, custom choices, faster service, a different style, or a fair price — not just by being the cheapest.

widgetConfig.scenario: There are already three other kids selling cookies at the school fair. What could help your stand stand out?

options.label: Offer something unique, like a special flavor or friendly branding
options.outcome: Great thinking! Standing out with something unique, even something small, helps customers choose you over competitors.

options.label: Copy exactly what the other stands are doing
options.outcome: Copying exactly what others do makes it harder for customers to choose you — offering something unique helps you stand out.

options.label: Give up since there's too much competition
options.outcome: Competition doesn't mean giving up — finding your own unique angle can help you succeed even in a crowded market.

slides.title: Word of mouth
slides.text: Happy customers telling their friends is one of the most powerful (and free!) ways a small business grows. For example, if one classmate loves the bracelet you made them and shows five friends at lunch, you might suddenly have five new customers without spending a single cent on advertising.

widgetConfig.scenario: One classmate loves your bracelet and tells five friends. What just happened?

options.label: Word of mouth brought new customers for free
options.outcome: Exactly! Happy customers telling their friends is one of the most powerful, and free, ways a small business grows.

options.label: This never helps a business grow
options.outcome: Word of mouth actually helps a business grow a lot, and it costs nothing.

options.label: You have to pay for every single new customer
options.outcome: Word of mouth is a free way to gain new customers — you don't have to pay for every one.

slides.title: Building a name people remember
slides.text: A consistent name, look, or feel for your business — sometimes called a brand — helps customers recognize and trust you again next time. For example, always using the same logo sticker and the same colorful packaging for your bracelets helps customers instantly recognize "oh, that's from her bracelet business" when they see it.

widgetConfig.scenario: You always use the same logo sticker and packaging for your bracelets. Why might this help?

options.label: It helps customers recognize and trust your business again
options.outcome: Exactly right! A consistent look or feel for your business helps customers recognize and trust you again next time.

options.label: Consistency never matters for a business
options.outcome: Consistency actually matters a lot — it helps customers recognize and trust your business over time.

options.label: Customers prefer a business that looks different every time
options.outcome: Constantly changing your look can make a business harder to recognize — consistency builds trust instead.

slides.title: Selling online with help
slides.text: With a parent's help, some young entrepreneurs sell crafts or art through simple online marketplaces, reaching far more people than a stand on the street. For example, a 12-year-old who makes custom drawings might, with a parent's account and supervision, list a few pieces online and reach buyers far beyond just their own neighborhood.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to sell your crafts online. What's the responsible way to do this as a kid?

options.label: Do it with a parent's help and supervision
options.outcome: Exactly right! Selling online as a kid should always be done with a parent's help and supervision.

options.label: Set it up entirely on your own without telling anyone
options.outcome: Selling online on your own without a parent's involvement isn't safe — always get help and supervision.

options.label: It's fine as long as you use a fake name
options.outcome: Using a fake name doesn't make it safe — getting a parent's help and supervision is what matters.

slides.title: Marketing on a budget
slides.text: You don't need to spend much money to market a small business — social media posts, flyers, and word of mouth can all work well for free or cheap. For example, posting a few photos of your bracelets on a family member's social media account, tagged with your prices, can reach dozens of potential customers without spending a single dollar.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to tell more people about your bracelets without spending money. What could work?

options.label: Posting photos on social media or word of mouth
options.outcome: Exactly right! Social media posts, flyers, and word of mouth can all work well for free or cheap marketing.

options.label: Marketing is impossible without spending a lot of money
options.outcome: Marketing doesn't have to cost much — free options like social media posts and word of mouth can work well.

options.label: You should never tell anyone about your business
options.outcome: Staying silent means fewer people ever find out about your business — low-cost marketing helps spread the word.

slides.title: Bundling and discounts
slides.text: Bundling means selling several items together for one combined price, often at a small discount compared to buying each separately. For example, offering three bracelets for $10 instead of $4 each encourages customers to buy more at once, while still feeling like a good deal for them.

widgetConfig.scenario: You offer three bracelets for $10 instead of $4 each. What is this pricing strategy called?

options.label: Bundling
options.outcome: Exactly right! Bundling means selling several items together for one combined price, often at a small discount.

options.label: Overpricing
options.outcome: This isn't overpricing — it's actually a discount for buying more at once, which is called bundling.

options.label: This has no name
options.outcome: This pricing strategy actually has a name — it's called bundling.

slides.title: Listening to customer feedback to improve
slides.text: Customers often give hints about how to improve your product, even when they don't realize they're doing it. For example, if several customers mention they wish your bracelets came in brighter colors, trying out a few brighter designs next batch could meaningfully boost your sales.

widgetConfig.scenario: Several customers tell you your cookies would be even better with less sugar. What's the smartest response?

options.label: Try adjusting the recipe based on the feedback
options.outcome: Great instinct — listening to repeated customer feedback and adjusting is exactly how businesses improve and keep customers happy.

options.label: Ignore it, your original recipe is perfect
options.outcome: Ignoring repeated feedback from multiple customers means missing a chance to improve your product and keep them happy.

options.label: Get upset that they didn't like it
options.outcome: Feedback isn't personal — it's useful information that can help make your product even better.

quiz.question: Three kids at school all sell friendship bracelets. Why might a business need to "stand out"?
choices: So customers have a reason to choose them specifically
Standing out never matters in business
quiz.explanation: When several people sell something similar, like three classmates all selling friendship bracelets, standing out gives customers an actual reason to pick you, such as custom colors or a better price. Without something different, customers have no reason to choose you specifically.

quiz.question: What is "word of mouth"?
choices: Happy customers telling other people about a business
A type of advertisement you have to pay a lot for
quiz.explanation: Word of mouth is customers telling friends about your business for free, and it's one of the most powerful kinds of marketing. If one classmate loves a bracelet and shows five friends, you might gain five new customers without spending a cent.

quiz.question: What is a "brand"?
choices: A consistent name or look that helps customers recognize a business
A random word with no meaning
quiz.explanation: A brand is a consistent name, logo, or look that helps customers recognize and trust your business again. Always using the same sticker and packaging for your bracelets helps people instantly know "that's from her bracelet business."

quiz.question: How might a young entrepreneur reach more customers than a street stand?
choices: Selling online with a parent's help
It's impossible to ever reach more people
quiz.explanation: With a parent's help and account, young entrepreneurs can sell crafts through online marketplaces, reaching far more buyers than a street stand ever could. A 12-year-old selling custom drawings online might reach buyers well beyond their own neighborhood.

quiz.question: A bracelet costs $3 in materials. Why might you price it at $8, not $20?
choices: It covers your costs and effort while still feeling fair to buyers
Higher prices are always better no matter what
quiz.explanation: A fair price covers your costs and effort without scaring customers away. If a bracelet costs $3 in materials, pricing it at $8 covers your work while still feeling reasonable for a handmade gift; $20 would likely feel like too much.

quiz.question: What does "bundling" mean, like offering three bracelets for $10 instead of $4 each?
choices: Selling items together for one combined, often discounted, price
Refusing to ever offer any kind of discount
quiz.explanation: Bundling means selling several items together for one price, usually at a small discount, like three bracelets for $10 instead of $4 each. It encourages customers to buy more while still feeling like a good deal to them.

quiz.question: Several customers mention they wish your bracelets came in brighter colors. What should you consider?
choices: Trying out their feedback to improve your product
Ignoring all customer suggestions completely
quiz.explanation: Customers often hint at how to improve your product without meaning to, like several people wishing your bracelets came in brighter colors. Trying out their suggestions in your next batch can genuinely boost your sales.

quiz.question: Why might a business offer a discount for buying in bulk?
choices: It encourages customers to buy more at once
Discounts always lose money with no real benefit
quiz.explanation: A bulk discount, like three bracelets for $10, encourages customers to buy more at once even though you earn slightly less per item. Selling more total items usually makes up for the smaller price each.

quiz.question: What's one downside of NOT having a consistent, recognizable brand?
choices: Customers might not recognize or remember your business
There are no downsides to skipping a brand at all
quiz.explanation: Without a consistent, recognizable brand, customers may forget your business or mix it up with someone else's. A memorable logo or packaging, used every time, makes people instantly recognize and return to you.

quiz.question: What's a safe way for a young entrepreneur to sell products online?
choices: Using a parent's account with their supervision
Setting up accounts secretly without telling any adult
quiz.explanation: Selling online safely as a young entrepreneur usually means using a parent's account with their supervision, not setting one up secretly. A trusted adult can help handle payments and messages from strangers safely.

slides.title: Profit and loss
slides.text: Profit is what remains when your business earns more than it spends; a loss happens when expenses are higher than earnings. If your dog-walking business brings in $60 but spends $75 that month, it has a $15 loss.

slides.title: Teamwork in business
slides.text: Many businesses run better with a team — different people handling different jobs, like making the product, selling it, and managing money. For example, if you and a friend start a dog-walking business together, one of you could focus on finding new customers while the other tracks the schedule and money — splitting the work makes it easier to grow.

widgetConfig.scenario: A business runs better with people handling different tasks based on their strengths. Why?

options.label: Because dividing tasks by strength helps the whole business run more smoothly
options.outcome: Exactly! Many businesses run better with a team, where different people handle different parts based on their strengths.

options.label: Teamwork never helps a business
options.outcome: Teamwork actually helps a lot — dividing tasks by strength makes the whole business run more smoothly.

options.label: Everyone should always do the exact same tasks regardless of skill
options.outcome: Assigning the same tasks to everyone regardless of skill wastes everyone's strengths — dividing by strength works better.

slides.title: Reinvesting in growth
slides.text: Instead of spending all the profit right away, many entrepreneurs put some of it back into the business — better supplies, a nicer sign, more inventory. For example, if your bracelet business earns $20 profit one week, using $10 of it to buy more beads and string for next week (instead of spending it all on yourself) helps the business keep growing.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your bracelet business earns $20 profit. What could help it keep growing?

options.label: Use some of the profit to buy more supplies
options.outcome: Exactly! Putting some profit back into the business, like more beads and string, helps it keep growing.

options.label: Spend all of it on yourself immediately
options.outcome: Spending all the profit on yourself leaves nothing to grow the business further — reinvesting some helps it keep going.

options.label: Reinvesting never helps a business grow
options.outcome: Reinvesting actually helps a business grow — using some profit for more supplies keeps things going.

slides.title: Handling a dissatisfied customer
slides.text: How you respond when a customer is unhappy can matter more than the original mistake — a calm, fair fix often turns a complaint into loyalty. For example, if a customer says their custom mug arrived cracked, offering a free replacement instead of arguing about it usually keeps them as a customer instead of losing them for good.

widgetConfig.scenario: A customer messages saying the item they ordered from your small business arrived damaged. What's the best response?

options.label: Apologize, listen, and offer a replacement or refund
options.outcome: Exactly right — handling complaints well turns an unhappy customer into a loyal one, and shows others you stand behind your product.

options.label: Ignore the message and hope they drop it
options.outcome: Ignoring complaints usually makes customers angrier and more likely to leave a bad review.

options.label: Tell them it's their fault for not being careful
options.outcome: Blaming the customer damages your reputation — a calm, helpful response protects your business's name.

slides.title: Teamwork and clear agreements
slides.text: When you run a business with a partner, agreeing early on who does what and how profits get split helps avoid arguments later. For example, two friends running a dog-walking business might agree in writing that one handles scheduling and the other handles the actual walks, splitting profits evenly between them.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two friends run a dog-walking business together. What helps avoid arguments later?

options.label: Agreeing early on who does what and how profits split
options.outcome: Exactly right! Agreeing early on roles and how profits get split helps avoid arguments later.

options.label: Never discussing how work or profits are divided
options.outcome: Not discussing this upfront often leads to disagreements later — agreeing early helps avoid that.

options.label: Agreements only matter after problems start
options.outcome: Waiting until problems start is too late — agreeing early helps prevent those arguments in the first place.

slides.title: Creating a simple budget
slides.text: A budget is a simple plan for how much money you expect to spend and how much you hope to earn or save over a certain time, like a month. For example, budgeting $20 for supplies and hoping to earn $50 in sales this month helps you know right away if you're on track or falling behind.

widgetConfig.prompt: Tap the budgeting steps in the right order
items: Set a goal for how much you'll earn

slides.title: When sales slow down
slides.text: Almost every business hits a slow stretch at some point, and how you respond matters more than the slowdown itself. For example, if candle sales drop for two weeks straight, checking whether your price, location, or scent selection needs adjusting is more productive than simply hoping things improve on their own.

widgetConfig.scenario: Candle sales drop for two weeks straight. What's the most productive response?

options.label: Check if price, location, or selection needs adjusting
options.outcome: Exactly right! Checking whether your price, location, or selection needs adjusting is more productive than just hoping things improve.

options.label: Just hope things improve on their own
options.outcome: Just hoping rarely fixes a slowdown — checking what might need adjusting is much more productive.

options.label: Give up on the business immediately
options.outcome: A two-week slowdown isn't a reason to quit — checking what needs adjusting is a better first step.

slides.title: Learning from a mistake
slides.text: Mistakes are one of the fastest ways to learn what actually works in a business, as long as you pay attention to what went wrong. For example, running out of cups halfway through a busy Saturday teaches you to buy extra supplies next time, turning a frustrating afternoon into a useful lesson.

widgetConfig.scenario: You ran out of cups halfway through a busy Saturday. What's the useful lesson?

options.label: Buy extra supplies next time
options.outcome: Exactly right! Running out of cups teaches you to buy extra supplies next time, turning a frustrating day into a useful lesson.

options.label: Mistakes teach you nothing
options.outcome: Mistakes actually teach a lot — this one shows exactly why buying extra supplies next time matters.

options.label: Never sell on busy days again
options.outcome: Avoiding busy days isn't the lesson here — the real lesson is to prepare with extra supplies next time.

quiz.question: A dog-walking business earns $60 in a month but spends $75. Was that month a profit or a loss?
choices: A loss, since it spent more than it earned
A profit, since $60 sounds like a lot of money
quiz.explanation: A loss happens when you spend more than you earn, even if the earnings sound decent alone. Earning $60 but spending $75 on flyers, leashes, and treats means that month actually lost $15.

quiz.question: What does "reinvesting" mean?
choices: Putting some profit back into growing the business
Spending every bit of profit immediately
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting means putting some of your profit back into the business instead of spending it all right away, like using part of a $20 profit to buy more beads for next week. It helps the business keep growing.

quiz.question: A customer's mug arrives cracked. What response is most likely to keep them as a customer?
choices: A calm, fair fix, like a free replacement
Arguing that it's not your fault
quiz.explanation: How you respond to a mistake often matters more than the mistake itself. Offering a free replacement for a cracked mug, instead of arguing whose fault it was, usually keeps that customer instead of losing them.

quiz.question: Why should business partners agree early on how profits will be split?
choices: It helps avoid arguments and confusion later
Profit splits never need to be discussed
quiz.explanation: Agreeing early on how profits will be split, and who does which job, helps business partners avoid arguments later. Two friends running a dog-walking business might agree upfront to split earnings evenly.

quiz.question: What is a simple budget?
choices: A plan for how much you'll spend, earn, and save
A list of your favorite snacks to buy
quiz.explanation: A budget is a simple plan for how much you expect to spend, earn, and save over a set time, like a month. Budgeting $20 for supplies while hoping to earn $50 helps you see right away if you're on track.

quiz.question: Sales have been slow for two weeks. What's a smart response?
choices: Look at what might be wrong and try adjusting, like price or location
Immediately shut the business down for good
quiz.explanation: Nearly every business hits a slow stretch at some point, and how you respond matters more than the slowdown itself. If candle sales drop for two weeks, checking your price, location, or scents is more useful than just hoping things improve.

quiz.question: You ran out of cups halfway through a busy Saturday. What should you do differently next time?
choices: Buy more cups ahead of time based on what you learned
Pretend it never happened and change nothing
quiz.explanation: Mistakes teach you what to fix next time, like running out of cups halfway through a busy Saturday. Learning from it means buying extra supplies next time instead of getting caught short again.

quiz.question: A candle business earns $100 and spends $130 on wax and wicks one month. Was that a profit or a loss?
choices: A loss, since it spent more than it earned
A profit, since $100 sounds like good money
quiz.explanation: A loss happens whenever you spend more than you earn, no matter how big the earnings sound by themselves. Spending $130 on wax and wicks while earning only $100 means that month lost $30.

quiz.question: Two partners disagree about how to split profits. What could have prevented this argument?
choices: Agreeing on the split before starting the business
There's no way to ever prevent this kind of disagreement
quiz.explanation: Agreeing on how profits will be split before starting a business prevents confusion and arguments once money actually starts coming in. Deciding this early, in writing if possible, protects the partnership.

quiz.question: Instead of spending all $30 of profit on candy, what's an example of reinvesting?
choices: Using some of it to buy more supplies for next time
Spending every single cent of it immediately
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting means using part of your profit to grow the business instead of spending every cent on yourself, like buying more supplies with some of a $30 profit. It helps next month's sales go even better.

slides.title: What is a business plan?
slides.text: A business plan lays out what a business will sell, who it's for, how it'll make money, and what it needs to get started — a roadmap for turning an idea into reality. For example, a teen wanting to start a pet-sitting business might write a one-page plan covering who their customers are (nearby pet owners), how much they'll charge per visit, and what supplies (a leash, treats, a scheduling app) they need first.

widgetConfig.scenario: Before starting a business, you write out what it will sell, who it's for, and how it'll make money. What is this document called?

options.label: A business plan
options.outcome: Exactly right! A business plan lays out what a business will sell, who it's for, and how it'll make money.

options.label: A report card
options.outcome: A report card is unrelated — the document describing a business's plan is called a business plan.

options.label: There's no need to plan anything before starting a business
options.outcome: Planning actually helps a lot before starting a business — that's exactly what a business plan is for.

slides.title: Startup vs. small business
slides.text: A small business is usually built to operate sustainably for its owners and customers. A startup is typically designed around a repeatable idea that can grow rapidly, often with significant uncertainty. A neighborhood pet-sitting service may be a small business; a platform built to connect thousands of sitters and pet owners across cities may be a startup.

widgetConfig.scenario: One business is built to grow rapidly and scale fast, while another is built to run steadily for its owner and customers. Which is typically called a "startup"?

options.label: The one built to grow rapidly and scale fast
options.outcome: Exactly! A startup is usually built with rapid growth and scaling in mind, while a small business focuses on sustainable, steady operation.

options.label: The one built to operate sustainably and steadily
options.outcome: That description fits a small business more — a startup is typically built around rapid growth and scaling.

options.label: There's no real difference between the two
options.outcome: There is a meaningful difference — startups aim for rapid scaling, while small businesses focus on steady, sustainable operation.

slides.title: Where funding comes from
slides.text: Businesses can be funded in different ways: personal savings, revenue from early sales, loans that must be repaid, or investors who provide money in exchange for ownership (equity). Each source changes the founder’s risk, control, and obligations.

pairs.right: Borrowed money that must be repaid
Money given in exchange for part ownership

slides.title: What does "scaling" mean?
slides.text: Scaling means growing a business to serve many more customers without everything becoming proportionally more expensive or difficult to manage. For example, a tutoring business that only earns more by adding more of the tutor's own hours doesn't scale well, but selling a recorded video course that hundreds of students can buy without extra work per student scales much better.

widgetConfig.scenario: A tutoring business only earns more by adding more of the tutor's own hours. A video course can be bought by hundreds of students with no extra work per student. Which one scales better?

options.label: The video course
options.outcome: Exactly right! The video course scales better since hundreds of students can buy it without adding extra work per student.

options.label: The tutoring business
options.outcome: The tutoring business doesn't scale as well, since earning more requires adding more of the tutor's own hours.

options.label: Neither one can ever scale
options.outcome: One of these actually does scale well — the video course, since it doesn't require more work per additional student.

slides.title: Finding your target market
slides.text: A target market is the specific group of people most likely to actually want and pay for what you're offering, rather than the entire population. For example, a business selling custom study planners is far better off targeting stressed high school juniors and seniors preparing for exams than trying to market to literally everyone.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to start a business selling trendy phone cases. Who should you research first before designing your product?

options.label: The specific group of people most likely to buy phone cases like yours
options.outcome: Exactly — understanding your target market's preferences and habits shapes smarter decisions about design, pricing, and marketing from the start.

options.label: Everyone who owns a phone, since anyone could buy one
options.outcome: Trying to appeal to literally everyone usually means appealing strongly to no one — a specific target market helps you design something people actually want.

options.label: No one — just make what you personally like
options.outcome: Your own taste matters, but understanding what your actual customers want is what turns a product into a successful business.

slides.title: Crafting a value proposition
slides.text: A value proposition is a clear, specific statement of why a customer should choose your product over any alternative, including doing nothing at all. For example, "Custom tutoring scheduled around your exact sports practice times" gives a busy student-athlete a concrete reason to choose you over a generic tutoring center.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're starting a tutoring business. What should your value proposition clearly communicate?

options.label: Why a student should choose your tutoring over other options
options.outcome: Exactly! A value proposition clearly explains the unique benefit you offer that makes customers choose you specifically.

options.label: A long list of unrelated personal facts about you
