options.outcome: A value proposition should focus on the specific benefit you offer customers, not unrelated personal details.

options.label: Nothing in particular, just vague positivity
options.outcome: A vague message doesn't help customers understand why to choose you — being specific about your unique value works much better.

slides.title: Market research basics
slides.text: Market research means gathering real information about what potential customers want, need, and are willing to pay, instead of just guessing. For example, sending a short survey to 30 classmates before launching a snack business can reveal that most would pay $2 for a granola bar, but not $5, saving you from mispricing later.

widgetConfig.scenario: You send a survey to classmates before launching a snack business. Why is this a smart move?

options.label: It reveals what customers actually want and will pay, instead of guessing
options.outcome: Exactly right! Market research gathers real information about what customers want and will pay, instead of just guessing.

options.label: Market research never helps avoid mistakes
options.outcome: Market research actually helps avoid costly mistakes, like mispricing a product customers wouldn't pay for.

options.label: Guessing is always better than asking customers
options.outcome: Guessing can lead to costly mistakes — asking customers directly, through research, gives much more reliable information.

slides.title: Choosing a business structure
slides.text: Businesses can use different legal structures, and the exact rules depend on where they operate. A sole proprietorship generally has one owner, while a partnership involves two or more owners. As a business grows, owners may consider other structures with help from a parent, accountant, or attorney.

widgetConfig.scenario: A business has exactly one owner. What is this type of structure generally called?

options.label: A sole proprietorship
options.outcome: Exactly right! A sole proprietorship generally has one owner.

options.label: A partnership
options.outcome: A partnership involves two or more owners — a business with exactly one owner is a sole proprietorship.

options.label: There's no name for this structure
options.outcome: There actually is a name for it — a business with one owner is called a sole proprietorship.

quiz.question: What is a business plan?
choices: A roadmap covering what a business will sell, who it's for, and how it makes money
A legal document required only for huge companies
quiz.explanation: A business plan is a written roadmap: what you'll sell, who your customers are, and how you'll make money. A teen starting a pet-sitting business might write one page covering nearby pet owners, a per-visit price, and supplies like a leash and scheduling app.

quiz.question: How does a startup typically differ from a small business?
choices: A startup usually aims to grow very fast with an unproven idea
There is no real difference between them
quiz.explanation: A startup is generally designed to test a repeatable idea that could grow rapidly, while many small businesses focus on serving a local or defined market sustainably. Either type can be successful; they simply have different growth goals and risks.

quiz.question: An investor gives $50,000 in exchange for 10% ownership. What did they get?
choices: A share of future profits or ownership
Nothing at all, ever
quiz.explanation: If an investor gives $50,000 in exchange for 10% ownership, the investor receives equity — a 10% ownership stake in the company. That is different from a loan, which normally must be repaid.

quiz.question: Why does a recorded video course "scale" better than one-on-one tutoring?
choices: It can serve many more customers without proportionally more cost or effort
Video courses are always cheaper to make
quiz.explanation: Scaling means a business can serve far more customers without its costs or effort growing at the same rate. A tutoring business that only earns more by adding the tutor's own hours doesn't scale well, but a recorded video course that hundreds can buy needs little extra work per student.

quiz.question: What is a "target market"?
choices: The specific group of people most likely to want your product
Every single person in the world, treated equally
quiz.explanation: A target market is the specific group of people most likely to actually want and pay for what you're selling, rather than literally everyone. A business selling custom study planners does better targeting stressed high schoolers before exams than trying to market to the whole population.

quiz.question: What is a value proposition?
choices: A clear statement of why customers should choose your product over alternatives
A legal document required to open a bank account
quiz.explanation: A value proposition is a clear, specific reason a customer should choose you instead of any alternative, including doing nothing. Telling a busy student-athlete "custom tutoring scheduled around your exact practice times" gives them a concrete reason to pick you over a generic tutoring center.

quiz.question: Why do businesses conduct market research before launching?
choices: To learn what potential customers actually want and will pay for
Because it's legally required before selling anything at all
quiz.explanation: Market research means actually gathering information about what customers want and will pay, instead of guessing. Surveying 30 classmates before launching a snack business might reveal most would pay $2 for a granola bar but not $5, saving you from pricing it wrong later.

quiz.question: What's the key difference between a sole proprietorship and a partnership?
choices: A sole proprietorship has one owner; a partnership has two or more
They are legally identical in every way
quiz.explanation: At the simplest level, a sole proprietorship has one owner and a partnership has two or more. The legal responsibilities, taxes, and registration rules can vary by location, so real businesses should check local requirements.

quiz.question: A teen uses $200 of personal savings to launch a t-shirt business instead of taking a loan. What's an advantage of this approach?
choices: They don't owe anyone money or interest if the business struggles
There is no real advantage to using personal savings
quiz.explanation: Using your own savings instead of a loan means you don't owe anyone money or interest if the business struggles. A teen spending $200 of personal savings on a t-shirt business risks only that $200, not a growing debt.

quiz.question: Which business idea would likely scale more easily?
choices: A print-on-demand online store
A one-person car detailing service that requires being there in person
quiz.explanation: A print-on-demand online store scales more easily because a printer fulfills each order automatically, without the founder doing more work per sale. A one-person car detailing service can't scale the same way, since the owner must physically be there for every single job.

slides.title: Pricing strategies
slides.text: Businesses generally price in one of two ways: cost-plus pricing, where you add a markup on top of what something costs to make, or value-based pricing, where you charge based on how much a customer believes it's worth. For example, a $5 material cost with a $10 markup gives a cost-plus price of $15, while a designer bag might sell for $200 largely because customers value the brand, not just the materials.

slides.title: Customer acquisition and marketing spend
slides.text: Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is the average amount a business spends on sales and marketing to gain a new customer. If it costs $20 to acquire a customer who creates only $15 of gross profit, the business may need to lower acquisition costs, improve margins, or increase repeat purchases.

widgetConfig.scenario: A business spends money on ads to get new customers. What is this average cost per new customer called?

options.label: Customer acquisition cost (CAC)
options.outcome: Exactly right! Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is the average amount a business spends to gain one new customer.

options.label: Customer lifetime value
options.outcome: That's a different metric — the average cost to gain a new customer is called customer acquisition cost.

options.label: There is no way to measure this cost
options.outcome: This cost can absolutely be measured — it's called customer acquisition cost (CAC).

slides.title: Measuring success beyond money
slides.text: Revenue matters, but it is not the only signal of a healthy business. Entrepreneurs may also track profit, cash flow, customer satisfaction, repeat purchases, growth, and impact. The right measures depend on the business and its goals.

widgetConfig.prompt: Sort each measure into Financial or Beyond money

slides.title: Competitive advantage
slides.text: A competitive advantage is whatever makes a business genuinely better or different from its rivals — often price, quality, convenience, or service. For example, a teen lawn-care business that guarantees same-day service, when every competitor takes a week to respond, has built a clear competitive advantage without needing to be the cheapest option.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two coffee shops sell similar coffee, but one consistently has longer lines. What might explain their competitive advantage?

options.label: They may offer something unique — better service, atmosphere, or quality
options.outcome: Exactly — a real competitive advantage comes from something genuinely hard for competitors to replicate, like exceptional service or a unique experience.

options.label: It's probably just random luck
options.outcome: Consistent success usually points to a real advantage, like service or quality, rather than just random chance.

options.label: Price is the only thing that could matter
options.outcome: Price matters, but plenty of competitive advantages come from service, quality, or experience, not just being the cheapest.

slides.title: Digital marketing basics
slides.text: Digital marketing means promoting a business online, through channels like social media, that often cost far less than traditional advertising. For example, posting short before-and-after videos of a car-detailing job can reach hundreds of potential local customers for free, something a printed flyer campaign could never do at that price.

widgetConfig.scenario: You post short before-and-after videos of a car-detailing job on social media. What's a benefit of this over a printed flyer campaign?

options.label: It can reach hundreds of people for little to no cost
options.outcome: Exactly right! Digital marketing, like social media posts, often costs far less than traditional advertising while reaching far more people.

options.label: Digital marketing is always more expensive
options.outcome: Digital marketing is usually far cheaper than traditional advertising, not more expensive.

options.label: Nobody ever sees posts on social media
options.outcome: Social media posts can actually reach hundreds of potential customers, often for free.

slides.title: Customer lifetime value
slides.text: Customer lifetime value estimates how much value a customer may generate over the whole relationship with a business. For example, someone paying $30 for a haircut about every six weeks for two years could generate roughly $500 in revenue — much more than the first $30 visit.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone pays $30 for a haircut about every six weeks for two years. What does this estimate of total value represent?

options.label: Customer lifetime value
options.outcome: Exactly right! Customer lifetime value estimates how much value a customer may generate over their whole relationship with a business.

options.label: A one-time purchase only
options.outcome: This is about the whole ongoing relationship, not just one purchase — that's what customer lifetime value measures.

options.label: This can't be estimated at all
options.outcome: This actually can be estimated — it's called customer lifetime value.

slides.title: Building loyalty and retention
slides.text: Retention means keeping the customers you already have coming back, which is usually cheaper than constantly finding new ones. For example, offering a simple reward, like a free car wash after every ten paid washes, gives existing customers a reason to keep returning instead of trying a competitor.

widgetConfig.scenario: You offer a free car wash after every ten paid washes. Why might this help your business?

options.label: It gives customers a reason to keep returning instead of trying a competitor
options.outcome: Exactly right! A simple reward like this gives existing customers a reason to keep returning instead of trying a competitor.

options.label: Rewards never affect whether customers return
options.outcome: Rewards actually do affect behavior — they give customers a reason to keep coming back.

options.label: It only helps new customers, not existing ones
options.outcome: This reward is specifically aimed at keeping existing customers coming back, not attracting new ones.

slides.title: Simple experiments (A/B testing)
slides.text: A/B testing means trying two versions of something, like two different ad photos or prices, to see which one performs better with real customers. For example, posting one ad with a photo of the product alone and another with it in use, then comparing which gets more responses, lets you improve with evidence instead of guesswork.

widgetConfig.prompt: Tap the A/B testing steps in the right order

quiz.question: Besides revenue, what else might an entrepreneur track as a sign of success?
choices: Customer satisfaction and real-world impact
Nothing else is ever worth tracking
quiz.explanation: Revenue isn't the only measure of success; entrepreneurs also track things like customer satisfaction and repeat business. A business with modest profit but 90% of customers returning again and again is often in a stronger position than one earning more but constantly losing one-time customers.

quiz.question: What's the difference between cost-plus and value-based pricing?
choices: Cost-plus adds a markup to cost; value-based charges based on perceived worth
They are exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: Cost-plus pricing adds a fixed markup on top of what something costs to make, like a $5 material cost plus a $10 markup equaling $15. Value-based pricing instead charges based on what a customer believes something is worth, like a $200 designer bag priced mainly for its brand, not its materials.

quiz.question: A business spends $20 to gain a customer who only spends $15. What's the problem?
choices: The cost of acquiring that customer is higher than what they spend
There is no problem at all
quiz.explanation: Customer acquisition cost is what a business spends, on average, to gain one new customer through advertising. Spending $20 on ads to gain a customer who only ever spends $15 is a losing strategy, even though the ad technically brought someone in.

quiz.question: What is a "competitive advantage"?
choices: Something that makes a business genuinely better or different than rivals
A random, meaningless name given to any business
quiz.explanation: A competitive advantage is something real that makes a business better or different from its rivals, like price, quality, or service. A teen lawn-care business guaranteeing same-day service, when every competitor takes a week, has a clear advantage without needing to be the cheapest.

quiz.question: Which is an example of low-cost digital marketing for a teen business?
choices: Posting product photos and videos on social media
Buying a national television advertising campaign
quiz.explanation: Digital marketing means promoting a business online, through things like social media, usually for far less money than traditional ads. Posting free before-and-after videos of a car-detailing job can reach hundreds of local customers, something a printed flyer campaign could never match at that price.

quiz.question: What is "customer lifetime value"?
choices: The total amount a customer is expected to spend over their whole relationship with a business
The price of a single item sold to them one time
quiz.explanation: Customer lifetime value is the total amount a business expects one customer to spend over their whole relationship with it, not just one purchase. A customer who gets a $30 haircut every six weeks for two years is worth roughly $520 in lifetime value, far more than that first $30 visit suggests.

quiz.question: Why might a business offer a loyalty reward, like "buy 9 washes, get the 10th free"?
choices: It encourages customers to keep returning instead of trying a competitor
Loyalty programs have no real effect on customer behavior
quiz.explanation: Retention means keeping customers you already have, which usually costs less than constantly finding new ones. Offering a free car wash after ten paid washes gives customers a concrete reason to keep returning instead of trying a competitor.

quiz.question: A business tries two different ad photos to see which gets more clicks. What is this called?
choices: A/B testing, a simple experiment to see what works better
Cheating, since only one ad should ever be used at a time
quiz.explanation: A/B testing means trying two versions of something, like two ad photos or two prices, to see which performs better with real customers. Comparing an ad showing the product alone against one showing it in use lets you improve decisions with evidence instead of guesswork.

quiz.question: A business has slightly lower revenue but 90% repeat customers, versus a rival with higher revenue but only 20% repeat customers. Which is often a sign of a healthier long-term business?
choices: Often the one with more repeat customers, reflecting lasting satisfaction
Whichever business made more money this month, automatically and always
quiz.explanation: A business with slightly lower revenue but 90% repeat customers is often healthier long-term than a rival with higher revenue but only 20% repeat customers, because repeat customers reflect real, lasting satisfaction rather than one-time luck.

quiz.question: A business spends $8 in ads to gain a customer who spends $50 over the next year. Is this a good outcome?
choices: Yes, the customer's value is much higher than the cost to acquire them
No, spending any money at all on ads is always a mistake
quiz.explanation: When a customer's expected value, like $50 spent over a year, is much higher than the $8 spent acquiring them, that advertising spending is working well. The business earns far more from the customer than it paid to reach them.

slides.title: Failure is part of the process
slides.text: Many successful entrepreneurs failed at a first (or second, or third) attempt. Learning from what went wrong is often what makes the next attempt succeed. For example, a teen's first attempt at selling custom phone cases online might flop due to poor photos and unclear pricing — but applying those exact lessons to a second attempt often leads to real success.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your first business idea didn't work out and you lost some money. What's the most useful mindset?

options.label: Figure out what you learned and try again smarter
options.outcome: That's the entrepreneurial mindset — most successful founders had failed attempts first. What matters is what you learn and do next.

options.label: Decide entrepreneurship just isn't for you
options.outcome: One failed attempt doesn't mean you're not cut out for it — nearly every entrepreneur has a failure story before success.

options.label: Avoid thinking about what went wrong
options.outcome: Avoiding the lesson means you're more likely to repeat the same mistake — reflecting on it is what turns failure into useful experience.

slides.title: Ethics in business
slides.text: Long-term success usually depends on being honest with customers, treating employees fairly, and not cutting corners just to make a quick profit. For example, honestly describing a product's condition, even when a vague description might sell it faster, builds the kind of trust that keeps customers coming back for years.

widgetConfig.scenario: A business is deciding how to treat its customers and employees for the long run. What usually drives long-term success?

options.label: Being honest and treating people fairly
options.outcome: Exactly! Long-term success usually depends on being honest with customers and treating people fairly.

options.label: Cutting corners and misleading customers whenever convenient
options.outcome: Cutting corners and misleading people tends to backfire — honesty and fairness drive long-term success.

options.label: Ethics has no connection to long-term business success
options.outcome: Ethics actually connects closely to long-term success — honest, fair treatment builds the trust businesses need to last.

slides.title: Solving a real problem
slides.text: The most durable businesses tend to solve a genuine problem for people — not just chase a trend that might fade quickly. For example, a tutoring business solving a real, ongoing need (students struggling with math) tends to last far longer than a business built around a fad that's popular for a few months and then forgotten.

widgetConfig.scenario: One business solves students' ongoing struggle with math, while another just chases a trend that's popular for a few months. Which tends to last longer?

options.label: The one solving a genuine, ongoing problem
options.outcome: Exactly right! The most durable businesses tend to solve a genuine, ongoing problem rather than just chasing a fading trend.

options.label: The trend-based business always lasts longer
options.outcome: Trend-based businesses tend to fade once the trend does — solving a genuine, ongoing problem lasts longer.

options.label: Both last exactly the same amount of time
options.outcome: They don't typically last the same — a business solving a real, ongoing problem tends to last much longer.

slides.title: Resilience and persistence
slides.text: Markets change, plans fail, and competitors appear. Entrepreneurs who adapt and keep going tend to outlast those who give up at the first setback. For example, if a new competitor undercuts your prices, adapting by improving your service or finding a new customer niche is more likely to succeed than simply giving up.

widgetConfig.scenario: A new competitor undercuts your prices. What's the more effective response?

options.label: Adapt by improving your service or finding a new niche
options.outcome: Exactly right! Entrepreneurs who adapt and keep going tend to outlast those who give up at the first setback.

options.label: Give up at the first sign of competition
options.outcome: Giving up right away misses a chance to adapt — entrepreneurs who keep adjusting tend to outlast those who quit early.

options.label: Ignore the competitor and change nothing
options.outcome: Ignoring a real competitive threat rarely works well — adapting your service or niche is a more effective response.

slides.title: Businesses that also help others
slides.text: Some entrepreneurs build 'social enterprises' — businesses designed to make money while also solving a social or environmental problem, not purely for profit. For example, a teen-run business that sells reusable water bottles and donates a portion of every sale to a clean-water charity is pursuing both profit and positive impact at the same time.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're starting a business and want it to also make a positive impact. What's one way to do that?

options.label: Donate a portion of profits to a cause, or use sustainable materials
options.outcome: Great approach! Many successful businesses build in a way to give back, which can also build customer loyalty.

options.label: Focus only on profit and ignore any other impact
options.outcome: You can focus on profit and still build in a positive impact — many customers actually prefer businesses that do both.

options.label: Wait until you're rich to think about giving back
options.outcome: You can start building in a positive impact from the beginning, even in small ways, rather than waiting.

slides.title: Handling complaints and protecting your reputation
slides.text: A single public complaint, especially online, can influence far more potential customers than just the one person who made it, so how a business responds matters enormously. For example, a business that quickly and openly resolves a customer's shipping complaint often earns more trust from onlookers than a business that has never had a complaint at all.

widgetConfig.scenario: A customer posts a public complaint about a shipping issue. What's the smartest response?

options.label: Resolve it quickly and openly
options.outcome: Exactly right! Quickly and openly resolving a complaint often earns more trust from onlookers than never having a complaint at all.

options.label: Ignore the complaint and hope it disappears
options.outcome: Ignoring a public complaint can let it influence more potential customers — resolving it quickly and openly works much better.

options.label: Argue publicly with the customer
options.outcome: Arguing publicly usually damages trust further — resolving the issue calmly and openly protects your reputation better.

slides.title: Splitting equity among co-founders
slides.text: When multiple people start a company together, they typically divide ownership — called equity — based on factors like who contributed the original idea, how much money each person invested, and how much ongoing work each will do. For example, two co-founders might split equity 50/50 if they contribute equally, or 70/30 if one invested significantly more money or works full-time while the other stays part-time.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two co-founders start a company — one invests significantly more money and works full-time, the other works part-time. What's a reasonable way to split equity?

options.label: Unevenly, like 70/30, reflecting the different contributions
options.outcome: Exactly right! Equity is typically divided based on factors like money invested and ongoing work, so an uneven split can make sense here.

options.label: Always exactly 50/50 no matter what each person contributes
options.outcome: Always splitting 50/50 regardless of contribution can feel unfair when one person invests much more — equity usually reflects actual contributions.

options.label: Equity never needs to be discussed or agreed upon
options.outcome: Equity actually needs to be discussed and agreed upon clearly, to avoid disputes later.

slides.title: Building a personal brand as a young entrepreneur
slides.text: A personal brand is the consistent impression you leave through how you present yourself and your work over time, both online and in person. For example, a teen who consistently posts high-quality photos of their baking under the same name and style becomes recognizable and trusted, which can open doors well beyond that one business.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teen consistently posts high-quality photos of their baking under the same name and style. What does this build over time?

options.label: A recognizable, trusted personal brand
options.outcome: Exactly right! Consistently presenting your work the same way over time builds a recognizable, trusted personal brand.

options.label: This has no effect on how people see their work
options.outcome: Consistent presentation actually has a big effect — it's exactly how a recognizable personal brand gets built.

options.label: Consistency only matters for big companies, not individuals
options.outcome: Consistency matters for individuals too — it's exactly how a young entrepreneur builds a personal brand people trust.

slides.title: Networking and mentorship
slides.text: A mentor is someone with more experience who can offer guidance, feedback, and warnings about mistakes they've already made themselves. For example, a local shop owner willing to spend twenty minutes answering a teen entrepreneur's questions about pricing can save that teen from repeating costly mistakes the shop owner already learned the hard way.

widgetConfig.scenario: A local shop owner spends twenty minutes answering a teen entrepreneur's questions about pricing. What is this shop owner acting as?

options.label: A mentor
options.outcome: Exactly right! A mentor is someone with more experience who offers guidance and feedback, like answering pricing questions.

options.label: A competitor
options.outcome: A competitor would be running a similar business for themselves — someone offering guidance like this is acting as a mentor.

options.label: An investor
options.outcome: An investor provides money for ownership — someone offering advice and guidance is acting as a mentor.

quiz.question: Why do many successful entrepreneurs talk openly about past failures?
choices: Learning from what went wrong often shapes what succeeds next
Failure has no useful lessons at all
quiz.explanation: Many successful entrepreneurs failed on their first attempt, and learning from exactly what went wrong is often what makes the next attempt work. A teen's first phone-case business might flop from poor photos and unclear pricing, but fixing those same issues next time often leads to real success.

quiz.question: Why does ethical behavior matter for long-term business success?
choices: Cutting corners for quick profit tends to damage trust over time
Ethics have no real impact on whether a business succeeds
quiz.explanation: Cutting corners for a quick profit, like vaguely describing a damaged product to sell it faster, tends to damage trust and hurt a business over time. Being honest, even when it's less convenient, builds the kind of trust that keeps customers coming back for years.

quiz.question: What tends to make a business durable over the long run?
choices: Solving a genuine, ongoing problem for people
Only ever chasing whatever trend is popular right now
quiz.explanation: Businesses solving a genuine, ongoing problem tend to last far longer than ones built around a passing trend. A tutoring business helping students who struggle with math addresses a lasting need, while a business chasing a fad that's popular for a few months tends to fade once interest does.

quiz.question: What is a "social enterprise"?
choices: A business built to make money while also solving a social or environmental problem
A business that only exists on social media
quiz.explanation: A social enterprise aims to earn revenue while also addressing a social or environmental problem. For example, a reusable-bottle business that donates part of its profit to clean-water projects combines a business goal with a mission.

quiz.question: Why does responding well to a public complaint matter so much?
choices: It's visible to many potential customers, not just the one who complained
Public complaints never affect other customers
quiz.explanation: A public complaint can be seen by many potential customers, so the response affects more than one person. A calm, transparent reply that fixes the problem can show others that the business takes customers seriously.

quiz.question: A competitor undercuts your prices significantly. What's a resilient response?
choices: Adapt, like improving service or finding a new customer niche
Quit the business immediately without trying anything else
quiz.explanation: Resilience means adapting when conditions change instead of quitting immediately. If a competitor cuts prices, you might improve service, focus on a different customer group, add value, or rethink your costs rather than automatically racing to the lowest price.

quiz.question: Two co-founders split equity 70/30 instead of evenly. What might explain this?
choices: One invested more money or works full-time while the other works part-time
Equity splits are always completely random, with no real reasoning
quiz.explanation: Equity, meaning ownership of a company, usually gets split based on how much money each founder invested and how much ongoing work they do. Two co-founders might split equity 70/30 if one invested significantly more money or works full-time while the other stays part-time.

quiz.question: Why might a young entrepreneur build a personal brand, like a consistent social media presence?
choices: It helps people recognize, trust, and follow their work over time
Personal brands have no real effect on a business's success
quiz.explanation: A personal brand is the consistent impression you build through how you present your work over time, both online and in person. A teen who consistently posts high-quality photos of their baking under the same name and style becomes recognizable and trusted, which can open doors beyond that one business.

quiz.question: Why is finding a mentor valuable for a young entrepreneur?
choices: A mentor can share experience and help avoid common mistakes
Mentors are only useful for adult business owners, never teens
quiz.explanation: A mentor is someone more experienced who can share guidance and warn you about mistakes they've already made themselves. A local shop owner spending twenty minutes answering a teen's questions about pricing can save that teen from repeating costly mistakes the owner already learned the hard way.

quiz.question: A business could quietly hide a small product flaw to sell faster, or disclose it honestly. Which builds a more lasting business?
choices: Disclosing it honestly, since that builds trust
Hiding it, since sales matter more than trust
quiz.explanation: Disclosing a small product flaw honestly, rather than hiding it to sell faster, builds the kind of trust that keeps a business's reputation intact over the long run. A business known for honesty tends to keep customers even when something occasionally goes wrong.
